Mores

/MOR-ayz/ - the stress falls on MOR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Mores means the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group.

Nothing in the dorm handbook covers it, but hall mores are strict: you do not run the blender during quiet hours, and you replace what you borrow.

Worked Example

In the county where my father grew up, mores govern a funeral more firmly than any statute: neighbors mow the family's lawn without asking, casseroles arrive unsigned, and nobody sells the bereaved anything for a month. No council passed these rules and no court could enforce them. Breaking one simply tells the town, permanently, what you are.

Mores is the precise term because these are the fixed customs and moral attitudes of a group — heavier than manners, which merely smooth social traffic. Skipping the casserole is not impolite; it is felt as a small failure of decency. That moral charge, enforced by regard rather than law, is what the word names.

How Mores Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

customs

customs: the usual practices, minus the moral charge

folkways

folkways: the everyday habits of a people, lightly held

Antonyms

lawlessness

lawlessness: no shared expectations holding at all

free-for-all

free-for-all: conduct with no common code behind it

How Strong Is It? — customs → mores → laws

customs vs. mores

customs vs. mores: Customs are the milder rung — what people usually do, like cake on birthdays; skip one and you are odd, not immoral.

laws vs. mores

laws vs. mores: Laws go further than mores: a law is written down and enforced by courts, while mores are enforced only by a community's regard — though losing that can hurt worse than a fine.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mor-

Root — mor-: custom, way (Latin mos)

Suffix — -es

Suffix — -es: Latin plural ending

Put it together

Put it together: Mor- (custom, way) + -es (Latin plural) = the customs, taken together. Latin mos meant a way of behaving; its plural mores meant the whole fabric of a community's ways. English borrowed the plural intact, pronunciation and all — which is why the word is always plural and rhymes with no English spelling of itself.

Use the root in a new word: moral

Root Check

Word Choice

academic / sociological

Mores is the sociologist's word — always plural, pronounced MOR-ayz — for the customs a group treats as matters of decency. Etiquette governs forks; mores govern what neighbors owe each other. Within this unit, keep the lanes: mores are what a community's conscience requires, ritualized describes the fixed form a practice has hardened into, and quotidian describes the everyday texture of what recurs.
